content: 1. Prothionamide is administered during the initial 4 to 6 months of treatment. 2. The second comparator is a long treatment regimen lasting 18 to 20 months, which does not include any of the newer tuberculosis (TB) drugs such as bedaquiline, delamanid, linezolid, clofazimine, or carbapenems. The intended duration of this regimen may not be achieved due to factors such as lack of treatment response, death, or loss to follow-up. For the purposes of analysis, long regimens are defined as those intended to last for 18 months or more. 3. The third comparator is a long treatment regimen lasting 18 to 20 months, which includes at least one of the newer TB drugs, such as bedaquiline, delamanid, linezolid, clofazimine, or carbapenems. Similar to the second comparator, the target duration may not be reached due to treatment non-response, death, or loss to follow-up. Long regimens in this context are also defined as those intended to last for 18 months or more. Regimens Excluded from Analysis: a. Short regimens lasting 9 to 12 months that do not conform to World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations and do not include bedaquiline. Patients receiving such regimens will be uniquely classified, and their characteristics and outcomes will be compared descriptively to those receiving other short regimens. However, they will be excluded from the primary analysis. b. Short regimens that include both bedaquiline and an injectable agent. Patients who begin such regimens but later switch to bedaquiline will also be uniquely classified. Their characteristics and outcomes will be compared descriptively to those receiving other short regimens, but they will be excluded from the primary analysis. Analysis of Outcomes: The study will evaluate eight distinct outcomes: i. Successful treatment completion. ii. Bacteriological cure at the end of treatment. iii. Adherence to treatment or treatment interruption due to non-adherence. iv. Treatment failure or relapse. v. Death during treatment. vi. Adverse reactions to anti-TB medications. vii. Acquisition or amplification of drug resistance. viii. Sustained bacteriological cure at least six months after successful treatment. Treatment failure and relapse will be combined into a single category, as will treatment completion and cure, which will be considered as treatment success. Odds of relapse-free treatment success will be estimated against various combinations of poor outcomes, and loss to follow-up (LTFU) will be analyzed separately against other outcomes. Adverse reactions and the acquisition of drug resistance cannot be analyzed using South African data, as this information is not routinely captured in the country’s EDRWeb system. Comparisons Analyzed: 1. Relapse-free treatment success (cure + treatment completion) up to 24 months post-treatment initiation versus failure/relapse. 2. Relapse-free treatment success up to 24 months post-treatment initiation versus failure/relapse and death during treatment. 3. Relapse-free treatment success up to 24 months post-treatment initiation versus all other outcomes (failure/relapse, death, and LTFU). 4. Loss to follow-up during treatment versus all other outcomes. The follow-up period of 24 months was selected to ensure comparable follow-up times for both regimens. The first patient in the analysis began treatment in January 2017, and follow-up ended in June 2019, resulting in a maximum follow-up period of 30 months. To maximize the study population for comparison, events occurring beyond 24 months will be censored. Sensitivity analyses will also examine outcomes at 18 and 21 months post-treatment initiation. Descriptive Analysis: Before addressing each research question, a descriptive analysis will be conducted for both the reference and exposure groups. This will include key characteristics such as age, sex, HIV co-infection, prior TB treatment history, and province of treatment. This analysis will help identify systematic differences between groups, differences in the geographic use of regimens, and provincial differences in treatment outcomes. The findings will inform further variables for matching or adjustment, such as the addition of a random effect for the province of treatment. Primary Analysis (South Africa Only): The primary research question is whether a bedaquiline-containing all-oral short regimen lasting 9 to 12 months achieves the same or better outcomes compared to the WHO-recommended short regimen lasting 9 to 12 months. The analysis will use a combination of exact matching and propensity score-based matching on several covariates to create comparable groups and minimize bias. Exact matching will be performed on HIV co-infection/ART use, prior TB treatment history, and the number of drugs to which the strain is resistant. Propensity score-based matching will include age, sex, and baseline sputum smear results. Logistic regression using mixed models will calculate adjusted odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals. Binomial regression will also be conducted to calculate adjusted risk differences. Secondary Analysis: The secondary research question is whether a bedaquiline-containing all-oral short regimen lasting 9 to 12 months achieves the same or better outcomes compared to long regimens lasting ≥18 months that include bedaquiline and/or delamanid. Sensitivity analyses will examine subgroups defined by the use of specific drugs or combinations of drugs. Limitations: 1. Drug resistance testing in South Africa relies primarily on genotypic methods, which may not detect resistance to drugs commonly used in short regimens (e.g., pyrazinamide, clofazimine, ethambutol, and ethionamide/prothionamide). 2. Baseline chest radiographic results, which may influence a clinician’s decision to use a short or long regimen, are not available and represent an unmeasured confounder. 3. Adverse events and the acquisition of drug resistance are not reported in the South African cohorts, precluding analysis of these outcomes. 4. Co-morbidities such as diabetes and mental health disorders are not routinely captured, limiting the ability to assess their impact on treatment outcomes. 5. Extrapulmonary TB is not included in the dataset and cannot be analyzed as a subgroup. 6. Bacteriological confirmation of cure or failure/relapse is rarely obtained, increasing the potential for observer bias. Conclusion: The study aims to compare the outcomes of various TB treatment regimens, focusing on relapse-free treatment success, adherence, and safety. Sensitivity analyses will address potential confounders and subgroup differences, while limitations such as missing data and unmeasured variables will be acknowledged.
